newsitem.title: GERMANY: German shops keen to open late as 40-year law goes.
newsitem.headline: German shops keen to open late as 40-year law goes.

text.p: Germany's shops will at last be able to stay open late from November 1, when a liberalised shop hours law replaces tight restrictions left over from the 1950s.
Both retailers and shop unions had long opposed the change, saying it would wipe out traditional corner shops, spoil workers' free time and upset family life.

But now surveys show about three-quarters of shops will take the chance to open until 8 p.m. on weekdays and 4 p.m. on Saturdays. The old weekday closing time was 6.30 p.m., with late closings on Thursday, and 2 p.m. on Saturdays.
The effect of the new hours will not be obvious immediately because on Friday, the first day under the new law, shops will be shut in Catholic regions of Germany for the All Saints Day holiday.

Even after that, however, retailers hold only modest hopes of boosting their turnover with longer hours. Most think big store chains that lobbied for the change will end up taking a larger slice of the retail pie away from local shops.
"I don't believe there will be a miraculous multiplication of money in people's wallets," said Holger Wenzel, head of the German Retailers Association (HDE).
In more service-oriented countries like the United States or Britain with competitive retail sectors, posters would likely be plastered on storefronts to lure shoppers during later hours.
Not so in Cologne. A walk down the Schildergasse, Germany's fourth busiest shopping street, revealed only a few small notices saying shops would observe the new closing times.
"We're not planning a promotion drive," Thomas Raeder of the City Marketing Cologne group told Reuters. "Total turnover won't rise. There will be just winners and losers."
But he said central Cologne retailers, which include department stores like Kaufhof, Karstadt and recently-opened Marks & Spencer, still hoped to win business by sticking to common opening times.
On Neusser Street, a typical busy shopping street with a full range of local stores in a Cologne suburb, owners have not agreed to coordinate opening hours to win passing trade.
The laundry will still shut at 6.30 p.m. and the optician has not made up its mind to open later.
And coffee shop manager Christa Schooss said she might stay open late three days a week but did not relish the prospect of a late walk to the metro. "Crime will just rise," she said.

Despite mixed feelings from retailers about the possibility of longer shop hours, the Munich-based Ifo institute said in a report: "Shop owners should not expect their readiness to adapt to be rewarded with higher turnover straight away. But over the long term longer hours will encourage consumers to spend more."
And consumers, long-suffering victims of bad service who see shopping as one of life's most stressful tasks, will welcome the chance to shop outside normal work times.
